note.value: JANE LEIGH PERROT TO MOUNTAGUE CHOLMELEY

text.p: London. September 11th. 1799
My dear Cousin,

Will it not surprise you to hear that the last month, from this very day, has been passed in real affliction without my giving you a line? I wished to spare you pain on my account and I hoped long before this to have written to you from my own comfortable House. I knew I must afflict you write when I would and I staid in hopes of being myself rather more equal to the task than I have lately been. You never imagined your Cousin would have addressed you from a Jail, and although I do not absolutely do that now , being in London in order to give Bail for my appearance at the Spring Assizes, yet my dearest Husband is not now my only Protector as I have the Ilchester Jailor in my suite - though to do him justice he has such a reliance on my honour, in spite of my appearances, that I scarcely ever see him, and since I have had the Honour of his acquaintance nothing can have been more respectful than his behaviour - Indeed we have every alleviation to our Misfortune that People can experience from the kindest Sympathy of Friends, and from the universal detestation the Authors of my troubles are held in by all ranks of People.

I must enter into a few particulars, my dear Cos, though you must have heard enough to make you in part acquainted with our situation. It is now five Weeks since I went into Smith's , a Haberdashers in Bath St; to buy some black Lace to trim a Cloak; when I had bought it the Shopman took it to the further part of the shop to put it up - this might have struck me as something particular had I not given the Man a £5 note to pay himself and bring me the difference - when he left me I turned from the counter to the door to catch my Goodman who in going to drink his Water generally passed that way. When the Man brought me my Change and the Parcel I left the Shop carrying the Parcel in my hand. I went homewards the same way that Parrot usually came and had not gone far before I met him, we went together to the Cross Bath, stopped to pay a tradesman's bill, and as we had a letter to put into the Post Office were going through Bath St; where I had an hour before bought my Lace, and when we came opposite the Shop the Woman who had sold me the Lace came across the Street and accosted me with these words, 'I beg pardon, Madam, but was there by mistake a card of white lace put up with the black you bought,' I answered I could not tell as I had not been home but she might satisfy herself as the parcel had never been out of my hand - on saying which
I gave it to her. She opened it, and there was a Card of White Edging which She took out saying Oh here it is,' and returned to the Shop. This did not surprise me as I thought it might have proceeded from Shop hurry or Negligence, but before we had got to the Abbey Church Yard the Man who had taken my Lace away to fold up, came after us to desire to know my Name and place of Abode as he had never put up that card of White Edging. This alarmed me a good deal because I had neither asked for White Lace nor had I seen any such thing in the Shop. Never hearing a syllable on the subject from the Thursday till the Monday Night I concluded they had discovered how their Mistake had originated, but on our return from passing Monday evening with some Friends the servant brought me a letter left by the penny post - without name or date, directed to Mrs. Leigh Parrot Lace dealer, No. 1. par. containing these lines "Your many visiting Acquaintance, before they again admit you into their houses, will think it right to know how you came by the piece of Lace stolen from Bath St; a few days ago. Your husband is said to be privy to it." On Wednesday following (the 14th) I was sitting up in my dear Parrot's Bed Chamber when my Maid came up and said a Gentleman in the Parlour wanted to speak to me. Judge of my horror upon going down to find he was a Constable with a Warrant from the Mayor for my immediate appearance. I went up to Parrot sick in Bed, and in profuse perspiration, who forgetting everything but my danger got up and attended me to the Mayor where we found these two Wretches who had sworn solemnly the One to seeing me take the Lace the Other to finding her Lace to the value of 20/s., in my possession - this she certainly did, but how it came there they best can tell as the first I ever saw of it was on the Woman's unfolding the paper with my black Lace. The Mayor and Magistrates, to whom we were well known, lamented their being obliged to commit me to prison on oaths of these People - they could only act in the capacity of Magistrates whatever their own private opinions might be - to prison I was sent - my dearest affectionate Husband ill as he was never left me - his tenderness has been beyond description. After above 17 Weeks confinement, with his large Shoe, and unable to move but with two Sticks, he has never seemed to have a thought but for me. We have had some unavoidable delays which have added to the painfulness of our situation - the Application for Bail could not be made because at this Season the Judges were only occasionally in London; - when we came to London we found no Person of our acquaintance here and though the four Sureties who were to join Parrot in
bailing me were found ready and happy to show their best services, and though substantial People (Worth and his Partners our Grocers) yet it was suggested that these malicious People might object to our Tradesmen, and therefore the Lawyer was sent to our own Parish and on his return assured us had fifty been required he could instantly have had them as everybody seemed eager to be the first in our Cause - this is pleasant my dear Cos: -

We shall be detained till after Monday as that is the first day the Judge can settle our business - I dread this close air more for Parrot than anything else - the House the Person who is with us uses is the Angel behind St. Clements. We did not care thinking we should be gone by this very day, and as we do not stir out nobody knows anything of us. My paper is full.
Accept our love and believe us dear Cos,
Your affectionate,
J. L. P.

note.value: JANE LEIGH PERROT TO MOUNTAGUE CHOLMELEY

text.p: October 10th. 1799 . Ilchester,
My dear Cousin,

Had I not been sure that your good sister would have told you all about us, I would have written to you long ago to have thanked you most cordially for your Affectionate Letter, and to have given you every information concerning my cruel disappointment after having like a School Girl told the intervening days between my imprisonment and my return to the Comforts of a home, which I have not now been at for 7 weeks. Indeed had it been possible for me to have painted the Scenes I have gone through during that period, and to have been certain of its continuance for so long a time, I verily believe every struggle would have proved ineffectual but I was flattered with the Idea of being only ten days here; so my trials have come on gradually but, God knows, I am so far from feeling inured to all I see and hear that, had the choice of Death or such a 7 weeks as the last been left to me (and no dearer object in view to stimulate my wish to live) I should not have hesitated one moment in determining on the first. Whether I may not have to pass the whole of the Winter here is at present uncertain - for after one Judge chose to refuse bailing me, whether from inexperience or profound Wisdom others must determine, why may it not be my Cruel fate to be remanded to Ilchester again? And was this to be the Case, I think I could not stand it - to be the wanton Sport of Malice and Villainy in every shape is too much to endure much longer
- and although the Newspapers have only reached as yet the Initials of my Name, they consider me now as fair game, and I shall travel for the future at full length I daresay. Oh, my Good Cousin, it may be to answer some wise purpose that such an atrocious Act, has gone so far, and I hope the Merciful disposer of Events will enable me to bear up in spite of such Affliction, but indeed I am not so far a good Christian as to refrain from wishing they may suffer all the horrors of a worse situation even than mine: Worse indeed it must be now, for their Conscience must be their most terrible accusers.

I hear that several similar Attempts have been made by the same Villain, and at the same Shop but none I fear with success enough to set the Wretch in his proper place . You cannot imagine how great a Comfort my old Friend Pen was to us. She was very kind, and in every respect what you would have wished her to be - her Humanity and Good Nature quite won her the Heart of my Jailor , or, as he is styled in Ilchester, the Governor , - (what would my poor Sister say to this) who declares he would go to London to fetch her if I was ill whilst here. This, if She knew the Man, is doing as much as the famous Lyre of Orpheus, for Stones and Savages would dance to Music as soon as he would hold Money cheap. I must keep very fair with him because I hear, and indeed sometimes from his own Mouth, that he has a number of Relatives and dependents who are always on the petty Jury and may do me favour or otherwise if he pleases. Good God! and am I to depend on so many People's good Opinion! Thank that God who lets me feel at peace with myself. I will enjoy that Idea let what may happen - this cannot be taken from me by a Malicious World.

One of my greatest Miseries here (indeed my very first) is the seeing what my dearest Husband is daily going through Vulgarity, Dirt, Noise from Morning till Night. The People, not conscious that this can be objectionable to anybody, fancy we are very happy, and to do them justice they mean to make us quite so; but all happiness is only comparative, and it is very fortunate that they are satisfied with their Life - to me a Day Labourer's lot with health and Bread and Cheese would be preferable to the Money they tell me this Governor acquires by His most honourable Employment . I had a long letter from my poor Sister the other day who seems to suffer sadly on our accounts. How many Worthy People have I caused distress to! how shall I ever feel grateful enough for the many real Friendships I have received! When I write, I paint my situation here in as fair a way as I can to her - she has few Comforts: I would not take from them, though I cannot add
at present to her happiness. I have a thousand Comforts in one - When I look upon the Man who seems to me from his Fortitude , his sweet serenity, and his Affectionate behaviour to have been sent as my Guardian Angel, my true Support under every Affliction, I am all Gratitude to the Almighty. After all, I would not change my situation, wretched as it appears to the World, for that Woman's whose Husband (if she loves as I do) happens to be out of the Kingdom, in the thickest of dangers, although She may be surrounded by everything the Gay World calls Happiness. What a letter I have written and all about this sad self - I think of you all my dear Cos; I rejoice in everything that tends to your Happiness, and wish you all a continuance of every earthly Comfort. I had an Account of each dear Relative from Pen: and the Account coming from her gave me true pleasure - pray tell her I shall write to her soon, but to you my dear Cousin I wished to write well knowing how anxiously you must feel for me. We are much better in health than I expected we should be - a Head Ache plagues me frequently, but my Heart aches so much oftener that I must not mention this lesser ill.
My dear Parrot desires his Affectionate Regards and wishes to yourself, Mrs. C... and our young Cousins - not forgetting dear Pen;
believe me ever most sincerely yours,
J. Leigh Parrot.

note.value: JANE LEIGH PERROT TO MOUNTAGUE CHOLMELEY

text.p: Ilchester, Nov. 10th, 1799.
My dear Cousin,

I fear my large sheet of paper will fright you, but I feel as if I had a vast deal to say and you have my leave when you have read till you are tired to lay my letter safe in Spider Hole and begin again at your leisure.

I had scarcely read your Letter (so long and so kind) when your Friend Maria and her Mother came into my Room - they were indeed most friendly in their behaviour and made me offer of Books, the produce of their Garden, or anything they could at any time contribute to our Comfort - but in truth, my dear Cousin, it is not in the power of anyone, let their benevolence be ever so great, to lessen materially the Many Evils we must unavoidably endure in this House of Misery. To say I thank you for your friendship in this introduction is not saying half enough - you must know what my grateful heart feels and therefore I shall not distress you more with Acknowledgements. I find Mrs. Goodford's Father, and family have conferred favours on this Man, and in some degree he is obliged to them for this place which, though a very shocking one to a Man of feeling must be a very lucrative one to such a Man as the one I now write of.

Mrs. G. took him out and told him that, as She should be coming two or three times a week and should probably bring other friends with her, it would be absolutely necessary that we should have a room to ourselves - this the Man seemed to take as a reproof and said he had on my first coming told me that the Dining Room I was to consider as my own whenever I choose to be alone - and so it was till Fires began; but this Room joins to a Room where the Children all lie, and not
Bedlam itself can be half so noisy, besides which, as not one particle of Smoke goes up the Chimney, except you leave the door or window open, I leave you to judge of the Comfort I can enjoy in such a Room. I have preferred sitting in our Bed Chamber and, as the Weather hitherto has not been very Cold, by keeping the doors shut I think it full as warm as the Dining Room with its open windows and doors; but as this
would not be the proper Room to receive Company in for more reason than one (N.B.) we have only one Chair and one Stool (I desired that, at our Expense ,

a Fire might be kept every day in the dining Room that I might, in spite of smoke, see Mrs. and Miss Goodford alone if they were so kind as to call on us - but even this Comfort I shall not enjoy, as your friend Maria (who kindly paid me a second Visit two days after her first) found me in my dining Room it is true, but the family there too - nor could their Ignorance let them see their impropriety in continuing there. And yet I dread anything that appears like discontent or Complaint made to my friends. Mrs. Goodford wonders at our not sending for our Servants, or at least for my own Maid - I could not tell her before these people that, though we were bearing a thousand disgusting Matters as to our Accommodations, Food, &c., my Servants would not, and I should have their murmurs added to our other troubles.

My Maid is a Welsh Woman with all the honesty and Passion of her Country - she would lay down her life to see me happy when she was not in one of her fits of passion ; but I am certain before she was in this house one week she would fight this swearing Vulgar Man and his Companions, nor could I, even knowing her to be right take her part in any contest - had my poor old quiet Chambers been living she would have been a real Comfort to me here ; but she never could have shown me more true affectionate duty and Respect than my present set of servants have done - indeed they are all highly spoken of by my numerous friends who write constantly from Bath. No! my Good Cousin, I cannot subject even a Servant to the sufferings we daily experience. We have rubbed through three Months and, though the next four may be more trying as the time of the year will be more against us, yet I put my trust in God and as Sterne makes his Maria say - "He will temper the Wind to the shorn Lamb" I hope. My dearest Parrot with his sweet composure adds to my Philosophy; to be sure he bids fair to have his patience tried in every way he can. Cleanliness has ever been his greatest delight and yet he sees the greasy toast laid by the dirty Children on his Knees, and feels the small Beer trikle down his sleeves on its way across the table unmoved. Your old guest Alderman Stonier was a Prince of Elegance to what we meet here. Mrs. Scadding's knife well licked to clean it from fried onions helps me now and then - you may believe how the Mess I am helped to is disposed of - here are two dogs and three Cats always full as hungry as myself.

You advise us to procure Bail, and who can doubt our
wish of doing this if it could be done with thorough safety at my future trial - but in order to procure Bail (after having been refused it) we have not only to produce the proofs we have of this Man's Negligence in Business, and some appearance of intended Frauds but copies of everything produced in Westminster Hall must be given to these Vile people - of course their counsel will have four Months to endeavour at counteracting all our evidence against him, - and should we not succeed I know I could never support being remanded here again - besides this, our Friend Mr. Hill advises that we should procure all our most Respectable Relations on each side to answer for me, as it would have a wonderful good effect on the Bench - but for what am I to draw all our happy Friends from their Familys? - Why! to save me the inconvenience of passing the next four months where we have passed the last three - Surely my dear Cousin this would be selfishness with a witness - If I was sure that my being so long imprisoned would prejudice a future Jury against me, I should certainly be sorry to lose any chance of an Honourable Acquittal; but I hope that there is more honour left than such prejudice would bespeak. I am more inclined to stay where I am than to run the risk of not succeeding - indeed I could not be happy anywhere whilst this thing hangs on my Mind. A public Court, and my appearance for a Capital Offence, you will allow are quite Antidotes to happiness. You will not my good Cousin like this letter one bit better than my last two - but I cannot dissemble with anyone much less with you - if I am angry all must know it - if I am miserable I cannot hide it. Mrs. Goodford was so good as to say I must come and see her, and she had enquired of the Man if he had any objection - the Answer - None at all - but I am resolved not to stir from this place as a Prisoner except by legal means. I have made my dear Husband promise me that, should she invite him , he will go - indeed I have a pride in letting the World see, and know the Man who thinks me deserving so much affection - besides which I think it may be of considerable advantage to him to get acquainted with some of the leading People in this Neighbourhood before the Assizes come on. I like your Friend Maria much - she seems sensible and feeling - as well as her Mother - we talked you all over at Easton - it happened odd enough but the day before your letter reached her Mrs. Philips (her Brother's Wife) had received a letter from Lady Napier at Bath to enquire whether there was not a Mrs. Leigh Parrot in this prison for the imputed crime of secreting Lace , begging to know how we were, and if we were well
accommodated - as we deserved every attention. Mrs. P. could give no answer then, now she knows who this Thief is, and may say something of me. Parrot joins me in kindest Love to Yourself and our circle of Cousins at Easton.

I shall write by the next post, or this if I have time, to my Sister, but I fear Pen: will have left Carlton before the letter reaches it. I hear a most pleasant account of you all - but this Gest comes too frequently on you.

I really think Steer's Opodeldock has strengthened Parrot's Sprained Ankle; he walks stouter - and is upon the whole better than I could have expected him to be. I have not been quite the thing this last week - anxiety of Mind is not good for Bowels naturally tender, I must not expect to be free from pains of the Body as well as mind - but I am ever most sincerely
Your affectionate Cousin,
J. Leigh Parrot.
P.S. Dallas, Jedge , and Bond are all retained as my counsel.

note.value: JANE LEIGH PERROT TO MOUNTAGUE CHOLMELEY

text.p: Ilchester, Jan., 1800.
My dearest Cousin,

That your Letters afford me real Comfort nobody that knows us both can doubt - Why then, say you, have I not sooner thanked you for your last truly kind one? At a Season too when everyone's good wishes are posting from Friend to Friend. That you have not one Relation or Friend in the World who more sincerely rejoices at your Happiness than myself is most true. I heard of your being surrounded by all your young Props , and in the most fervent prayer did I beg a Continuance of every blessing to you and them, but as my letter could not add one Moment to your Comfort I could not O my kind Cousin! Why should I pain you by telling you of my Griefs! and yet I could not with truth write pleasantly of my dearest Parrot for some time past; I thank God he is now better but for one whole Night, and all the Next day, did he lie in such an Agony of Pain, that my distress was cutting indeed. I was desirous of having the Medical Man of Ilchester, though my Heart ached at the Alternative, (as his trades are Apothecary, Surgeon, Coal dealer, Brick and Tile Maker, &c. , which seemed to bespeak his being good at None) but the dread of his mistaking the Constitution, so naturally full of Gout and the Assurance from my poor Sufferer that he knew it was a severe fit of Gravel, or something like it, (I hope not
Gall Stones by the acuteness of pain) made us give this Assistance up, and as he has been better for the last two or three days my mind is a little easier on his Account. I had a Comfortable kind Letter from Good Pen, yesterday. She writes in good spirits, but talks of London being visited by terrible Colds and Coughs - I think One I have got would match any she writes of. -

My Sister is writing to inform me of the Addition to her Carlton Comforts - in her last letter she informs me of my having a powerful Champion in your dear John at some Meeting where a Mr. Casamajor chose to tell my strange story - and adding that he had heard particulars from his Relation by Marriage , Sir William East, who was much shocked at it. If he had heard from Sir W. E. I will answer for it he never heard anything said unhandsome of us, for Sir W. on hearing from Payne of Maidenhead how I had been used lamented his being obliged to leave Berkshire the next day for Lady East's health which prevented his offering himself as one of my bail and wished it lay in his power to be of any service as well through the Regard he felt for us as to show his detestation of so much Villainy, for almost a similar Case had nearly involved Lady East in the distress that I was thrown into. Miss Molly Casamajor may love Scandal as well as other Creatures of his description. - Pray thank my Cousin John and tell him I trust I shall never make him blush at having taken up my defence.

I find Miss Goodford is coming to visit your Young Married Woman - She is very friendly to us indeed, and if dreadful Roads were not between us I know she would be a very great Comfort to me. Mrs. G. and her friend Mrs. Daniell a most interesting pleasant Woman, made us a long Morning Visit a few days ago. She seems as warm and friendly in her Attentions as if I were her near Relation. You mistake the Matter my dear Cousin when you fancy my Servants have objections to coming here - they wished to come - but one of my Comforts is that I am so truly independent now (suffering so much when poor old Chambers died) that I want no Attendant - when my dear Parrot is ill in Bath, my only pleasure is to attend him myself - besides here is a very respectable Servant in this Family who has attached herself so much to us, that I should have nothing for my Servants to do and I am sure I could not improve them in any one instance here.

I hear from them every Week. and they are of some use there, as my old Friends are very frequent in their Enquiries
and Messages. I should like to see you hobbling about though I confess two sticks are not advantageous to the Gait. - We have not left off our two yet, though I think our Ankle gains considerable Strength, more owing to keeping it uncommonly warm than to any Medical Applications. I see Mrs. Blundels name amongst those friends who called on me in Bath last week. I suppose she is full of talk of her Brother's gay Choice. I do not think he will dislike a Card playing, Rout going Wife at all - if I was his Lady I should like distraction a little more than I now do. You will not expect any amusing Anecdotes from hence - in truth I never yet have seen so truly miserable a place as this same Ilchester - I make up however in Affection what I may want as to Life or Spirit for I can truly subscribe myself.
Your Sincere and Affectionate
J. Leigh Parrot.
P.S. Pray remember to circulate our kindest Love and Good Wishes to your Fire Side and to Mrs. Johnstone's if they have left Easton.

note.value: JANE LEIGH PERROT TO MOUNTAGUE CHOLMELEY

text.p: Ilchester, March 6th, 1800.
My dearest Cousin,

You have heard from your good Sister some account of my sufferings within the last three weeks; I shall not pain you by the repetition but tell you that I am now comparatively happy in seeing this Treasure of my Life in a Convalescent State. I hope he will leave off the use of James' Powder tomorrow, and, if this sad Cold weather does not prevent him get about in the Air again.

Mr. Watts has taken a House for our Witnesses at Taunton, and says he thinks he shall have to procure 10 or 12 more beds as fresh People were coming forward every day to offer their services - even the very day before he was here he had a Gentleman called to say he would step forward to prove a similar trick in his family at the Shop . This ruinous Expense is what we shall long feel - but we are not expensive People and believe me, Lace is not necessary to my happiness.
Adieu my dear Cousin. Accept Parrot's and my most affectionate wishes and ever believe me
Your sincere
J. L. P.

note.value: JANE LEIGH PERROT TO MOUNTAGUE CHOLMELEY

text.p: Bath, April 1st, 1800.
My dearest Cousin,

Once more I address you unprison'd , but oh! how I have been wrung! - to the very quick believe me. You will rejoice to hear that I was most honourably acquitted - but you will grieve with me that we cannot punish my Vile Antagonists. Let it however comfort us that, if his own Conscience acquits him, he is in the high Road to punishment, most likely to the Gallows. The Circumstances, which my Trial brought out, are sufficient Grounds against him on his Perjured Bankruptcy Business; and some of the Persons then present have promised to do for him. I own what partly consoled me for what I had undergone was the delightful Idea of the Pillory Exhibition for my pretty pair of Lovers - but my Solicitor says nothing can be done. You heard from your Friendly Sister what a Scene of Hurry and Confusion we lived in. ... I fear She was most uncomfortable and I wished her not to be out of the House - bad as it was, it would have been as well as a Lodging out - but She would not have a Bed such as we could offer - indeed I felt myself greatly obliged to her for her kind Appearance. From her you heard how many Witnesses we had taken down. Three out of three and twenty I believe were examined, and were sufficient to prove Mr. Filby Rogue enough in all conscience. I never heard of so vile a Character but I fear he had so many nearly as bad as himself, that swearing black was white seemed nothing to them. Mr.
Justice Laurence behaved handsomely, he wished me seated, and sent several times to signify such wishes - and he sent Mr. Jekyl to repeat (in a louder Voice than my Agitation would allow of) any Observations I wished to make to the Judge after the Evidence Against me had been examined; but I must at the same time confess that (unless I was partial to my own Cause) he did not let enough be said of Filby's Villainy - he thought enough had been said to fully clear me, and was pretty sure that the winding up of his Charge to the Jury would put every doubt respecting my Innocence out of the Question; but I think it was a dangerous Experiment. My oath was not betaken; my Husband's Evidence in my favour was nothing - else I could have disproved my having on any Cloak, though the Villain swore he saw the Lace under my black Cloak - several similar Perjuries (had we not been Man and Wife ) might have been proved. The Judge, after he had said everything respecting Filby's Deposition as well as the others, added "And now you have heard all this, if you can believe Filby's Evidence, if you should be inclined to believe His Evidence, I have only to desire you to consider the Attestations of those Gentlemen who have attended on behalf of Mrs. Leigh Parrot's Character." He then repeated each kind Friend's testimony, and their knowledge of me for many years in their own words, which were all as highly gratifying as possible. The Jurymen, who seemed much more enlightened than Petty Jurors generally are took Notes many of them and were 7 Minutes and half studying to explain those Notes to their less intelligent companions, before they brought me in not Guilty - a clapping of hands to show Approbation and Joy immediately began, which the Judge hushed as not being allowable - so this Vile Matter rests.

Lord Braybrook, Vansittart, Annesley and Grant, with four Bath Friends kindly attended us. Never tell me of Erskine, Garrow , or any of your Popular Counsellors; my Friend Bond was animation all over - and preserved the Gentleman at the same time, which some of your great Men cannot always support. I was disappointed in Jekyll - Dallas was very well. Pell had little to say but he showed vast feeling by perfectly sobbing whilst my Observations were repeated. Indeed I never saw so many Men weep. I have taken a large sheet thinking to transcribe them for your entertainment - you were with me in thought the whole time I know. The frightful Expense I cannot Estimate. I am told it will be nearer two than one thousand pounds and from the large demands already made only for conveying the Witnesses (and the two days Expenses for the House and Eating at Taunton which alone amounted to £93; odd money), I can easily suppose it will be full that sum. What a comfort that we have no Children!
My Lord and Gentlemen of the Jury,

I am told that my Counsel cannot be permitted to address
to you any remarks on my Case. The Circumstances of it do not render it necessary to detain you long, but as my Counsel are prevented I cannot (although nearly unequal to the speaking in such an Assembly) help taking advantage of this Opportunity. Placed in a Situation in every respect the most Enviable - blessed with a Tender and most Affectionate Husband who is ever anxious to indulge my Wants and anticipate my Wishes and whose Supply of Money is so ample as to leave me rich after every desire is gratified what inducement could I have to commit this offence? Depraved indeed must have been my Mind if with these Comforts I could have been tempted to this Crime. You will hear from my Noble and highly respectable Friends what has been my conduct, and what has been, and still is their opinion of me. Can you think it possible they have been so many years deceived? Is it possible that at this time of Life my disposition should so suddenly change and that I should foolishly hazard the well earned reputation of a whole Life by such Conduct, or endanger the Peace of Mind of a Husband for whom I would willingly lay down that Life? You have heard their Evidence: I shall not, nor indeed can I make any comments upon it: I leave that where I am satisfied it will be used with Justice and Mercy. I will only ask you whether to be found opposite to the Shop within the space of little more than half an hour, and with the Lace in my Hand is like the conduct of a Guilty Person. My Oath is on this occasion inadmissible; but I most solemnly assure you and I call on that God, whom we all acknowledge and adore, to reward or punish me as I now speak true or false and to witness my Assertion, that I did not take the White Lace knowingly from Smith's Shop, nor had I any reason to suspect or believe that the same was in my Parcel when accosted by my Prosecutrix."

As soon as the Trial was over, the Adversaries hastened to Bath that they might circulate the story they had fabricated. The Paragraph inserted in the Paper was "that after a long trial and the clearest and most Satisfactory Evidence from the Prosecutrix and Witnesses the Jury were more than half an hour out of Court when they brought the Verdict in not Guilty." It was reported too that I had fainted and was carried out of Court - that another Trial was carried on, and then I was brought in again, tried by a fresh Jury which had all been bribed with a guinea each and they acquitted me. You see my dear Cousin how fertile a Spot Bath is. The Author of the Erroneous Paragraph was made to own it erroneous and, in handbills distributed about, to promise the true statement. We did not reach Bath till 12 o'Clock on Sunday Night and before
10 on Monday Morning our anxious Friends began coming in so that till Bed time I could not get a Moment to write you this Account. I thought I would be early enough to-day, but no such thing, my whole time has been taken up in kissing and Crying. The post is now gone and I could cry to think you should be so many days in hearing from us. May I soon hear that you are quite well, and that dear Mary has made you a Grand-papa . Give our kind love to Mrs. Cholmeley and my Young Cousins. I have written you a monstrous long letter and yet I feel as if I had not said half I meant to say. I have written to Pen: at Yeovil - She will tell you a great deal about us I daresay. Accept our best love, and believe me
Your Affectionate
J. L. P.

note.value: JANE LEIGH PERROT TO MOUNTAGUE CHOLMELEY

text.p: Bath. April 8th, 1800.
My Dear Cousin,

To be sure (as a kind Friend told me) I stand some chance of being killed by Popularity - though I have escaped from Villainy. The more I reflect on the diabolical Set that swore such abominable Falsehoods the less I wonder at the Numbers that swing every Year - indeed I am almost led to fear that many Innocent People suffer from false Oaths. That these Wretches had marked me for somebody timid enough to be Scared, and Rich enough to pay handsomely rather than go through the terrible Proceedings of a public Trial nobody doubts; and by timing it when I had only my Husband with me there were sure that I could have no Evidence against them. Surely our boasted Laws are strangely defective - owing to this Circumstance I find no Punishment from me can attach to this Villain - and had he gone off the very day before the Trial, we should have lain under the Stigma of having bought him off without a possibility of Clearing ourselves. We had been put to a very great Expense in collecting Witnesses from London to prove frauds in his Bankruptcy Business - from Birmingham to bring out Circumstances which the Judge stopped proceeding on or it might have hanged him. Query did he not richly deserve the Gallows? A fine sum it will cost, and all that we have for it is that the Solicitor for the Bankruptcy assured us he should lay hold of him, and from what he had on my Trial discovered made no doubt of his meeting the fate his Villainy to me deserved without any other Crimes.

I think we have left so many Friends at the Castle that if our Debts - or another Filby , should drive us there we shall stand a good chance, nay it was told Parrot by a Person of some Shrewdness that he would stand a very good Chance if he would offer for Ilchester at the ensuing Election. What a noble finish this would be to our Jail Adventures would it not?
J. L. P

note.value: JANE LEIGH PERROT TO MOUNTAGUE CHOLMELEY

text.p: Bath. April 14th, 1800.
My dearest Cousin,

Thank you, my good Cousin, for your Letter. We begin to feel more Calm - but the more Calm I feel (though perhaps a a contradiction) the more ruffled I am with all the People principally concerned in this most infamous Transaction. I agree with you about not being quite satisfied with any but Bond; and he would, I am convinced, if the Judge had not stopped him have made that Villain Filby squeak pretty loud. I cannot help thinking (and I suppose this must be quite entry nous ) that the Judge acted very wrong. I may lean too much on my own Side because I know my Innocence and the horrid Roguery of this Set of Perjured People - but I think Judge Laurence leant as much on the other side. He, it is alleged, knew he could in drawing up his Charge show his opinion of my Innocence in his last three or four lines - but to 9 out of ten Petty Jurors this was a dangerous Experiment. Such a Set of Jurors were hardly ever known - they even took Notes - and this accounts for their being above a quarter of an hour in explaining those Notes to those amongst them who were more unenlightened. Why the Judge should stop Mr. Bond when he was showing to the whole Court that Filby was the greatest Villain that ever existed - and not only Perjury but other matters of ye most serious consequences could be brought against him I know not - but this I do know that, if I had been allowed to speak and had been equal to the Exertion, I should have proposed a few questions which would have been I think unanswerable - first why, if the Man saw Lace secreted under my Cloak, did he let me, a perfect Stranger, quit the Shop? That I had no Cloak on was only to affirm what I could bring only my Husband to prove - so that is nothing. I confess when I came into Court and found that the Perjury seemed deeply connected and that not only the Prosecutrix and Filby (her sole Witness as I thought) but the very Shop Girl was in the same strange Story, I was struck with horror to see how far Wickedness might proceed. Yet for myself I felt no ill consequence. I find now that the greatest censure is thrown on the Mayor - and in my opinion he deserves it. It appeared to us unaccountable that we should never have heard anything for a whole week after this Transaction. The Prosecutrix swears that, on her seeing me pass on the opposite side of ye Street in half an hour afterwards, She went out, and upon my giving her the Parcel and saying, if there was white Lace put up with the black I had bought, it must be through the Negligence of her Shop Man. She answered "It is no such thing, it is no such thing you stole it" - Can anyone believe that all this could have been said to me in one of the most public streets in Bath - at two o'Clock when everybody was passing to the Cross Bath to drink the Water and that no person should have heard it which she says was the Case? Can anyone believe that if She had dared to have said this to me My Husband (whom
She says answered only "No she did not") would not have taken some legal steps against such defamation of a Wife's Character? Her words were so very different to what She swears , that I could not even suppose it an Accusation - though She says it made me turn Scarlet . When the Man came after me to know our Name: I own then a presentiment of intended Villainy flashed on me, and then I should not have wondered at turning Scarlet or any Colour of the rainbow. We wondered that some Knavish Attorney had not made his Appearance next Morning to have frighted me, but never could I suspect that they were so deep in their Scheme as to have gone to the Mayor; however they swear they did - and they were put off on various Excuses. We have heard that the Mayor knowing our Mode of Living, and our respectable Characters, did full as much as he ought to prevent their proceeding in the Business - but why did he not through some Friend let us know the premeditated Perjury and give us an opportunity of consulting our Lawyer? And another Query of the greatest Consequence is why did he on asking the People at the Town Hall who were in the Shop and hearing that there were two Shop Girls at work which two Girls he sent for immediately, but discharged them in five minutes on one saying She was quite out of hearing, and the other (Rains) saying She only heard me ask for the Lace I had cheapened the Day before, and nothing more, why I say did he not take this in writing or why (now that he finds these Girls both Called upon, and Rains swears to every Particular in which She has been tutoring these 7 Months) does he not state everything as it happened in the Town Hall before him? As to our wish of punishing the Man, who can doubt it! but your Idea of the Case being the same as if I had been called a Thief in a public Paper is I am told by Lawyers quite wrong. - then I could only get redress by proceeding against him, and the King's Bench with ample damages might have been the Consequence. But now a public Court and an honourable Acquittal is much more satisfactory to the whole World - and how can we blacken those People more than they have blackened themselves - the Man is off and the Shop I hear must be ruined. All this my dear Cousin I could not help writing you, though I greatly fear it will make your Head ache to read it. You can have no Idea how very warm and Friendly everybody seems to us. Everyone of our old and our new Acquaintance are coming to us continually - by sitting for seven hours in the Court with wet feet I brought a very bad cold to Bath - attended with one of my bad Coughs.
Bath is not the place to lose these disorders in - my dear and Affectionate Sister Austen is impatient for our getting into Hampshire, but I cannot go just yet. I shall not feel quite easy till our heavy Charges are known and paid . I think by the time they are paid, my dear Husband may assert with truth that he is not worth one penny in right of his Wife - I wish I may be mistaken. I find the Carlton Family set forward on their London expedition on the 21st; Pray my dear Cousin do not fancy that I am ever too deeply engaged in any Business or pleasure not to write to you. Never can I forget your warm and Affectionate Zeal. I could not regard you more than I did before, but little did I think to have proved your Friendship in so trying a Cause. God bless you all. Our kind love to you and yours.
Believe me
Your sincere and faithful friend
J. Leigh Parrot.
